questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Good course catalogues and a place you find interesting. Also, with decent accommodation available.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Finding it was easy enough, but the systems didn't always make sense or were user-friendly.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had help from a counsellor who helped me switch courses during my first weeks.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: A lot of student accommodation places outside of the host institution were extortionately highly priced and demanded payment until mid-July, when you're already home. My roommate, who was a fellow exchange student, and I booked a long-term Airbnb, which was pricey but worth the cost for the accommodation and convenience. It was much easier to book than other student accommodation sites. I would recommend it if you are planning on living with another exchange student, like a partner or friend.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: You'll partly miss out on the experience of living with other students. However, those accommodations are usually worse than what you can find elsewhere, albeit less pricey. If you make friends with people at those accommodations, then you can partly experience it through them. You might live further away from campus as well, so you need to find a place where you can still easily get to the campus and inner city.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was easy for me because I got the courses that I wanted on the first try.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You were sent a survey in which you filled out information about the course you wanted. You only needed three courses, but you could submit four courses, and you would either get fewer than three of those and have to send in new courses, get three precisely or get all four and have to drop one of them when you arrive.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could only email and hope to get a quick response, which could vary.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful, although I changed my courses when I arrived.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You need to brace yourself for the fact that you might not get what you want precisely due to class capacity or timetable clashes. Therefore, have a bunch (10 or more) courses pre-approved.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took year two and year three courses, or level 2 and 3 as they were called in England. One of my courses also had level 6 students on them. You get quite a bit more maturity out of those courses than first-level courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The seminars or tutorials were a lot shorter than those at home. In general, there was less teaching, but still high quality.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Phonology (LELA20012)
Experimental Phonetics (LELA32022)
Hegel and Marx (PHIL23022)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend phonology and experimental phonetics if you are interested in that area, as you learn a lot of interesting topics from very intelligent professors. I would also recommend Hegel and Marx if you are interested in that topic, as the teacher was incredible.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Drinking and eating. Tram.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Produce was actually a lot cheaper than I expected here. Shopping at supermarkets and making food at home could easily be done on a budget. Transportation for students is pretty cheap, at least with buses through the Bee Network. Trams were separate, though. Ubers are cheap too as an option

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I participated in softball as part of the Sporticipate program, which was great, albeit short. I engaged in some events by different societies, which I would recommend checking out. I also became friends with other exchange students, and joined group chats were wocial things were planned. There is a lot of opportunity for social engagement as an exchange student if you want to involve yourself. There are societies and day trips to places (Wales, York, etc.), plenty of stuff to do if you look them up.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Sportiticapte, as you register for one pound, you can then participate in all sorts of sports from softball to archery. You can find all sorts of societies with special interests for people who are like-minded to you or have similar interests, and they do a lot of events. The students' union and campus have a lot of opportunities for social engagement. It's up to you to involve yourself. Other exchange students are keen to do it too, so get amongst it.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I had a lot of fun visiting small towns nearby (Stockport, Didsbury) and making bigger trips (Wales, Liverpool, York, London). These are sometimes offered on the student union website and are cheaper than going yourself, as trains are expensive here. An alternative is Flixbus, which is cheaper but slower. I would recommend doing what you want to, but don't stay home all weekends; there are great pubs and social opportunities in the city, which you can explore with the friends you make. Explore the whole city and the places surrounding it on day trips or longer. You have three weeks of holiday in the non-teaching period. So fill it out with visits or fun plans.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, as England is very similar to Denmark culturally. You might find the accent weird of youre not familiar. The biggest thing is just the traffic. How it is on the other side of the road, how they seldom have pedestrian crossings outside of the inner city and how people are pretty reckless as pedestrians.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Honestly, I mostly talked to other exchange students outside of some I was placed in a group project with. However, if you want to, I'm sure there are a bunch of local students who want to get to know you. You probably have to take the initiative, though; a good starting point is the people in your course, as they are interested in the same things as you. So start with that and take it from there. Or engage in societies and sporticipate.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: How local students disregard showing up on time or listening to lectures. The local students didn't seem to care about what they were studying. Classes could often be pretty small. They are also younger than most Danish students and therefore more immature. There's also a lot of vaping, which you have to get used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Pub culture. Being generally more polite to strangers (thanking the bus driver, asking how you're doing)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Attendance doesn't matter as much as they tell you; you need to have a below-40 % attendance rate for them to take it seriously. Go to your courses, but don't stress about going to all of them.
Use the reading spaces and libraries as they are excellent for studying and getting sources.
Visit museums around the city (a lot are free), and join societies and sporticipate for socialising.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Find out if you need to travel by bus often, and if you do, then get a student term card on the Bee Network app. Try to see what workshops and pop-up shops, etc., are happening at the students' union. And remember, everyone is there for the same reason as you, so put yourself out there if you want to engage with other exchange students. Everyone is normally super nice. Get to know Manchester, as a city, as it will become your home. Take the studying seriously and learn, but don't waste time trying to get perfect grades. You only need to pass, and have it be transferred as a pass back home, and getting 40% (which is a pass) is very easy. So relax and enjoy the experience of exchange and don't lose yourself in the schoolwork. You're here once, and it's a big process and very expensive, so enjoy the time you get here. It's over before you know it

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting a second home abroad, learning new things in a different place with different opportunities, and meeting amazing people.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Honestly, the exchange itself is easy, other than some processes in the beginning. The hard part is the entire application leading up to it. That is way harder than being here. Once everything is sorted, you go on as if you're home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
